o: On day d you must buy the currently cheapest remaining item of whichever shop you pick, paying value * d. You choose the shop order. By the rearrangement/exchange argument, the optimal schedule buys the globally smallest values on the earliest days: if a larger value were bought before a smaller one, swapping their days increases the total. So flatten all m*n values, sort ascending, and pay the i-th smallest value multiplied by (i+1).
k: Exchange argument: assigning larger multipliers (later days) to larger values maximizes the sum.
Since each shop exposes its minimum remaining item, any global ascending assignment is realizable by always picking the shop holding the current global minimum.

a.n: Sort flat values and multiply by day index
a.i: Collect all values, sort ascending, and sum value * position. Any such assignment is feasible because on each day the shop containing the next needed value offers it as its rightmost available item.
s: Flatten the matrix into one list.
a.t: O(mn log(mn)) — sorting the flattened values dominates.
a.sp: O(mn) — flattened copy (could be O(1) extra with a heap over row pointers).

w: An equivalent implementation merges rows with a min-heap, popping the global minimum m*n times — same complexity class, useful if rows arrive as streams. Watch 64-bit accumulation: up to 1e5 values * 1e6 * 1e5 days exceeds 32 bits. Common pitfall: trying to greedily simulate shops day by day without proving the exchange argument. Follow-up: minimize spending instead (assign large values to early days).
